lessons.title: The Ending & Key Themes
lessons.description: Macduff vs Macbeth, the fulfilment of prophecies, the restoration of order under Malcolm, and a thematic overview of the whole play.
lessons.content_html:
The Final Battle: Scenes Seven to Nine

The closing scenes of Macbeth build rapidly towards the final confrontation. Shakespeare switches between short scenes inside Macbeth’s castle and scenes following Malcolm’s advancing army, creating a pace that generates tension and excitement. Macbeth compares himself to a bear tied to a stake: ‘They have tied me to a stake; I cannot fly, / But, bear-like, I must fight the course.’ This is a reference to bear-baiting, a blood sport held in arenas next to the Globe Theatre. The bear is chained and cannot escape — it must fight or die. Macbeth recognises that he is trapped by fate, yet chooses to go down fighting rather than surrender.

When Macbeth kills Young Siward, he boasts: ‘Thou wast born of woman. / But swords I smile at, weapons laugh to scorn, / Brandish’d by man that’s of a woman born.’ His confidence in the witches’ prophecy makes him arrogant and reckless. Shakespeare deliberately places this boast just before Macduff enters — the one man who was not ‘of woman born.’ The audience feels the dramatic irony tightening.

Key Fact

Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane when Malcolm orders his soldiers: ‘Let every soldier hew him down a bough / And bear’t before him.’ The soldiers carry tree branches as camouflage. This fulfils the third apparition’s prophecy in a way Macbeth never imagined. Shakespeare shows that the witches told the truth — but in a way designed to deceive. This is situational irony.

Macduff vs Macbeth

When Macduff confronts Macbeth, he calls him ‘Turn, hell-hound, turn!’ The compound noun ‘hell-hound’ combines the imagery of damnation with a hunting dog — Macbeth has become a demonic, predatory creature. A hound pursues and hunts relentlessly, suggesting Macbeth’s tyranny has been an unrelenting assault on Scotland. The alliteration in ‘hell-hound’ makes the insult sharp and percussive, heightening the drama of the moment.

Macbeth initially refuses to fight Macduff: ‘Of all men else I have avoided thee. / But get thee back; my soul is too much charged / With blood of thine already.’ The word ‘soul’ is significant — Macbeth still has enough conscience to acknowledge the weight of his crimes against Macduff’s family. But this could also be a taunt: ‘I have already destroyed your family; there is no need for more.’ Macduff’s response is devastatingly simple: ‘My voice is in my sword.’ Words are no longer enough; only action will deliver justice.

The Prophecy Fulfilled: ‘Untimely Ripp’d’

Macbeth declares ‘I bear a charmed life, which must not yield / To one of woman born.’ Macduff’s reply shatters his confidence: ‘Despair thy charm; / And let the angel whom thou still hast served / Tell thee, Macduff was from his mother’s womb / Untimely ripp’d.’ Macduff was delivered by Caesarean section — technically not ‘born’ of woman in the natural sense. The prophecy is fulfilled, but not as Macbeth expected.

Macbeth’s reaction is a moment of anagnorisis — the tragic recognition. He curses the witches: ‘And be these juggling fiends no more believed, / That palter with us in a double sense; / That keep the word of promise to our ear, / And break it to our hope.’ The word ‘double’ echoes through the play — ‘double trust’, ‘double, double, toil and trouble’ — and now Macbeth finally understands that the witches’ equivocation has been his undoing all along. Banquo’s warning from Act One is proved right: ‘The instruments of darkness tell us truths, / Win us with honest trifles, to betray’s / In deepest consequence.’

Shakespeare was influenced by Aristotle’s writings on Greek tragedy. Two key concepts apply to Macbeth:

Peripeteia (the reversal): There are several candidates — Duncan’s murder, the banquet scene, or the moment Macbeth learns Birnam Wood is moving. Each marks a point where Macbeth’s fortune shifts irreversibly.

Anagnorisis (the recognition): When Macbeth learns Macduff was ‘untimely ripp’d’, he realises the witches have deceived him. He accepts his doom but chooses to fight: ‘Yet I will try the last.’ This final act of defiant courage is a trace of the brave warrior from Act One, making his death both tragic and oddly noble.

Malcolm’s Final Speech: Restoring Order

Macduff enters carrying Macbeth’s severed head and declares: ‘Behold, where stands / The usurper’s cursed head: the time is free.’ The word ‘free’ signals the end of tyranny. Malcolm is proclaimed King of Scotland and delivers a speech that restores order. He promotes his thanes to earls — ‘the first that ever Scotland / In such an honour named’ — rewarding loyalty just as his father Duncan did. He calls home those exiled by ‘the snares of watchful tyranny.’

Crucially, Malcolm describes Macbeth and Lady Macbeth as ‘this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen.’ ‘Butcher’ reduces Macbeth to a mindless killer, while ‘fiend-like’ associates Lady Macbeth with the Devil. These labels are Malcolm’s political narrative — but the audience knows the characters are more complex than these simple summaries. The play’s tragedy lies in the fact that Macbeth was once a ‘valiant’, ‘worthy gentleman’ and Lady Macbeth was once a devoted partner who was ultimately destroyed by guilt.

Key Fact

Malcolm’s coronation at ‘Scone’ — the traditional site of Scottish coronations — symbolises the restoration of the Great Chain of Being. The rightful king is back on the throne, Scotland is healed, and the natural order is restored. This ending would have pleased King James I, reinforcing the message that challenging the Divine Right of Kings leads to destruction.

Thematic Overview: The Whole Play

For the exam, you need to be able to discuss the play’s key themes across all five acts. Here is a summary of the most important themes and how they develop.

Ambition: Macbeth’s hamartia (fatal flaw). The witches’ prophecies ignite it, Lady Macbeth fans it, and Macbeth acts on it. The play asks: is ambition itself evil, or only when it leads to immoral action?

Kingship & Tyranny: Three kings: Duncan (virtuous but naive), Macbeth (tyrannical), Malcolm (wise and just). Shakespeare presents a spectrum of rule, with Macbeth as the warning against disrupting the Divine Right.

The Supernatural: Witches, prophecies, apparitions, ghosts, hallucinations. Do the witches cause Macbeth’s downfall, or does he choose his own path? The play balances fate and free will without giving a definitive answer.

Guilt: Tracked through the blood and hand-washing motifs. Macbeth’s guilt evolves from horror (‘Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood?’) to resignation (‘I am in blood, stepp’d in so far’) to nihilism (‘signifying nothing’). Lady Macbeth’s guilt evolves from denial (‘A little water’) to madness (‘Out, damned spot!’).

Appearance vs Reality: ‘Fair is foul and foul is fair’, ‘look like the innocent flower but be the serpent under’t’, the witches’ equivocal prophecies, Malcolm’s test of Macduff. Nothing in Macbeth is what it seems.

Masculinity: Lady Macbeth equates manliness with violence (‘unsex me here’). Macbeth adopts this view. Macduff challenges it: ‘I must also feel it as a man.’ Shakespeare presents toxic masculinity as destructive and emotional honesty as true strength.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the exam, if you get an extract from the final scenes, make sure you discuss how the ending resolves the play’s key tensions. Link Malcolm’s ‘dead butcher and fiend-like queen’ back to the characters’ complexity throughout. If asked about fate vs free will, use the final battle to argue both sides: the prophecies are fulfilled (fate) but Macbeth chose to seek out the witches and act on their words (free will). Always end your essay with a clear, concise statement about Shakespeare’s overall message — e.g. ‘Shakespeare warns that unchecked ambition, combined with the corruption of the supernatural, leads to the destruction of both the individual and the state.’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The prophecies are fulfilled through situational irony: Birnam Wood ‘moves’ as camouflage, Macduff was ‘untimely ripp’d’ by Caesarean. Macbeth’s anagnorisis comes when he realises the witches ‘palter with us in a double sense.’
  • Malcolm’s coronation restores order: he is the wise, just king that Scotland needs. His summary of Macbeth as ‘this dead butcher’ is politically convenient but overly simplistic — the audience has seen Macbeth’s full tragic arc.
  • For exam revision, know the six key themes (ambition, kingship, supernatural, guilt, appearance vs reality, masculinity), track each one across all five acts, and always link to Jacobean context (Divine Right, Great Chain, Gunpowder Plot, witchcraft beliefs).

practice_questions.text: Read the following quotation from Act 5 Scene 8: ‘And be these juggling fiends no more believed, / That palter with us in a double sense.’ How does Shakespeare use Macbeth’s language here to present ideas about equivocation and the supernatural?
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for developed analysis:
• ‘Juggling fiends’ calls the witches deceitful devils — ‘juggling’ means trickery, ‘fiends’ means demonic beings (1)
• ‘Palter with us in a double sense’ means they spoke with double meanings — technically truthful but designed to mislead (1)
• ‘Double’ echoes through the play: ‘double trust’, ‘Double, double, toil and trouble’ — the theme of deception comes full circle (1)
• This is Macbeth’s anagnorisis — his moment of tragic recognition that he was deceived. He finally understands Banquo’s warning about the ‘instruments of darkness’ (1)
• Links to Jacobean context: equivocation was a major concern after the Gunpowder Plot (1605) (1)

Max 4 marks.
